reels.title: A day on Venus is longer than its year
reels.hook: One spin of Venus takes longer than its whole trip around the Sun.
reels.caption:
A day on Venus is longer than its year. 🪐

Venus turns so slowly that one spin on its axis takes about 243 Earth days. One trip around the Sun takes only about 225.

And it spins backwards. If you could see through its thick clouds, you'd watch the Sun rise in the west and set in the east.

Which fact got you: the day or the sunrise? 👇

Follow for more facts that sound fake but aren't.

Source: NASA Science, Venus facts.
reels.alt_text: A 3D-animated Venus with swirling pale-yellow clouds turns slowly in space, then is shown orbiting a glowing Sun before the Sun rises over its edge. Bold captions read "1 day > 1 year?", "1 spin = 243 days", "1 orbit = 225 days" and "Sunrise: west".

reels.title: You've never seen the Sun as it is right now
reels.hook: Sunlight takes 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach you, and Andromeda's light left before our species existed.
reels.caption:
You've never seen the Sun as it is right now. ☀️

Its light takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach you, so you always see it a little in the past. The farther you look, the older the light.

The Andromeda galaxy is visible to the naked eye from a dark site, and its light left about 2.5 million years ago. Our species has been around for roughly 300,000 years.

Would you rather see the Sun live or Andromeda as it is today? 👇

Sources: Smithsonian (How Things Fly), NASA Hubble (M31), Smithsonian Human Origins.
reels.alt_text: A 3D animation: the blazing Sun, a pulse of light racing to a small Earth, a pull-back through the stars to the Andromeda galaxy, then a night horizon under the sky. Bold captions read "The Sun · 8 min ago", "8 min 20 s late", "Farther = older", "2.5 million years" and "Before humans existed".

sources.name: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum: How long does it take light from the Sun to get to Earth?

reels.title: A ball of iron under your feet as hot as the Sun
reels.hook: Earth's centre is about 6,000 °C, as hot as the Sun's surface, and pressure keeps it solid.
reels.caption:
There's a ball of iron under your feet as hot as the surface of the Sun. 🌍🔥

In 2013, researchers in Grenoble squeezed iron between two diamonds and found Earth's centre is about 6,000 °C (give or take 500). The Sun's surface is about 5,500 °C.

The pressure down there, over 3 million atmospheres, keeps that iron solid. The heat stirs the liquid iron around it, and that stirring makes the magnetic field your compass follows.

Which surprises you more: the heat or the pressure? 👇

Sources: ESRF (Anzellini et al., Science 2013), NASA Sun facts.
reels.alt_text: A 3D animation: Earth with a wedge cut away to show glowing layers and a white-hot inner core, a comparison with the Sun, then blue magnetic field lines looping around the planet. Bold captions read "As hot as the Sun", "~6,000 °C", "Sun's surface: 5,500 °C", "3+ million atmospheres" and "Heat makes the magnetic field".

reels.title: Saturn would float in water
reels.hook: Saturn is nine times wider than Earth, yet on average it's less dense than water.
reels.caption:
Saturn could float in a bathtub. 🪐🛁

It's about 9 times wider than Earth, but it's mostly hydrogen and helium, so its average density is less than water's.

That makes it the only planet in our solar system that would float, if you could find a tub big enough.

Which would you rather see: Saturn in a bathtub or Saturn up close? 👇

Follow for more facts that sound fake but aren't.

Source: NASA Science, Saturn facts.
reels.alt_text: A 3D-animated Saturn with golden bands and wide rings floats on a calm sea, is compared in size with a small blue Earth, then bobs in the water before the camera pulls back to reveal a giant bathtub. Bold captions read "Could Saturn float?", "9× wider than Earth", "Less dense than water" and "The only planet that floats".

reels.title: A sugar cube of neutron star
reels.hook: One sugar cube of neutron star material would weigh about a trillion kilograms.
reels.caption:
One sugar cube of neutron star material would weigh about a trillion kilograms. 🧊⭐

A neutron star is the crushed core left behind when a giant star dies. It packs around half a million Earths of mass into a ball only about 20 km across, roughly the size of a city.

What would you compare a trillion kilograms to? 👇

Follow for more facts that sound fake but aren't.

Source: NASA Goddard, Imagine the Universe: Neutron Stars.

Bold captions read "1 sugar cube = ?", "~1 trillion kg", "500,000 Earths in 20 km" and "A star the size of a city".

reels.title: More trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way
reels.hook: About 3 trillion trees on Earth; 100 to 400 billion stars in our galaxy.
reels.caption:
Earth has more trees than the Milky Way has stars. 🌲✨

A global study in Nature estimated about 3.04 trillion trees. Our galaxy holds somewhere between 100 and 400 billion stars, so there are at least seven trees for every star.

And that count only includes trunks at least 10 cm wide.

Did you think it would be the other way round? 👇

Follow for more facts that sound fake but aren't.

Sources: Crowther et al., Nature (2015); ESA; NASA Goddard.

reels.title: Sink to the deepest point on Earth
reels.hook: Mount Everest would disappear underwater in the deepest part of the ocean.
reels.caption:
Mount Everest would disappear underwater in the deepest part of the ocean. 🌊

Sunlight fades by 200 m and is gone by 1,000 m. Most animals down there make their own light. Every night, trillions of them rise to feed: the biggest migration on Earth. The Titanic lies at 3,800 m; past 6,000 m is the hadal zone, named after Hades. The deepest fish ever filmed, a snailfish, was seen at 8,336 m in 2022. Researchers think that's near the limit for fish. Challenger Deep bottoms out around 10,935 m, at over 1,000 atmospheres. Two explorers first reached it in 1960 in the Trieste. Everest (8,849 m) would sit about 2 km under the surface.

Even there, a camera found a plastic bag (10,898 m). And less than a third of the seafloor has been mapped in detail.

Which stop surprised you most? 👇

Sources: NOAA Ocean Service, NOAA Ocean Exploration, MBARI (Martini & Haddock 2017), UWA (via NPR), Seabed 2030.

reels.title: Why is the sky blue?
reels.hook: On the Moon, the sky is black. Even at noon.
reels.caption:
On the Moon, the sky is black. Even at noon. 🌑

Earth's air is the difference. Sunlight holds every color, and air molecules scatter short wavelengths most. Violet (400 nm) scatters about ten times more than deep red (700 nm).

So why isn't the sky violet? Sunlight has less of it, and our eyes are less sensitive to it.

Did you expect violet to win? 👇

Sources: NASA; Royal Museums Greenwich; Physics FAQ.
reels.alt_text: A cut-paper animation. A blue sky is torn open to show an astronaut under a black Moon sky. A sunbeam fans into colored strips, paper molecules scatter them, ten violet cards outnumber one red card, and paper layers turn the sky to sunset.

reels.title: Why neon glows
reels.hook: Most neon colors contain no neon at all.
reels.caption:
Most neon colors contain no neon at all. 💡

Neon gas glows reddish-orange. Electricity pushes electrons through the gas, they hit atoms, and the atoms give the energy back as light.

Blue comes from argon with a little mercury, often with a coating too. Many other colors come from powder inside the glass that turns ultraviolet into visible light.

Which sign color would you pick? 👇

Sources: Edison Tech Center; Wikipedia (Neon sign, Neon).
reels.alt_text: An animated neon sign lights up red on a rainy brick wall, then the view goes inside the tube where dots representing electrons and a ring-shaped atom glow. Blue, pink, green and white signs light up in turn, before the neon-free ones switch off.

reels.title: Why is Mercury so hard to reach?
reels.hook: This spacecraft took eight years to reach Mercury.
reels.caption:
Eight years to reach Mercury. 🛰️

The Sun's gravity keeps pulling a spacecraft faster, and go too fast and you can't stop. So BepiColombo swung past Earth once, Venus twice and Mercury six times before entering orbit on November 21, 2026.

A software glitch ended its engine burn early, leaving a 75-hour orbit instead of 58. ESA says no extra burns are needed. The two orbiters are due to separate December 9–10.

Would you have waited eight years? 👇

Sources: ESA; WRAL (NASA Ambassador Tony Rice).
reels.alt_text: Cut-paper animation. A spacecraft with blue solar panels falls toward a huge yellow Sun, flies past Mercury, then swings by Earth, Venus and Mercury before circling Mercury and splitting into two orbiters.

reels.title: 245 animals in one rock
reels.hook: 245 animals lived in this one rock.
reels.caption:
One deep-sea rock, 245 animals. 🪨

Scientists examined 244 fist-sized nodules from the Pacific seafloor, 4 to 6 km down, and found 4,139 animals. The average was 17 per rock. One held 245.

The rocks grow a few millimeters in a million years, and they're rich in metal.

Mine them or leave them? 👇

Source: Scientific Reports (2026), via MARUM and ScienceDaily.
reels.alt_text: Cut-paper animation of a dark seafloor rock covered in tiny colorful animals, compared with a fist, shown deep in the Pacific, then lifted by a yellow mining claw.

reels.title: How El Niño changes winter
reels.hook: Warm water in one place can bring rain far away.
reels.caption:
Warm water in one place, rain far away. 🌧️

In El Niño, Pacific trade winds weaken and warm water moves back toward the Americas. The jet stream shifts south. The Gulf Coast and Southeast tend wetter, and the northern U.S. tends warmer and drier.

Forecasters put the chance of strong to very strong El Niño lasting through January–March 2027 at roughly 80% (November 19 update). That's odds, not a promise.

What's winter doing where you are? 👇

Sources: NOAA; Drought.gov.

reels.title: Same Question, Different World 2: Rain
reels.hook: There is a world where it may rain iron.
reels.caption:
There is a world where it may rain iron. ☄️

On Earth, rain is water. On Titan, at −179 °C, methane makes the rain, rivers and seas. On WASP-76b, winds carry iron vapor to the cooler night side, where astronomers suspect it condenses and falls.

Same Question, Different World, part 2. Part 1: why our sky is blue and the Moon's is black.

Next: sunsets. Which world should we visit? 👇

Sources: NASA; ESO.

reels.title: Is water wet?
reels.hook: Is water wet? Science and the dictionary disagree.
reels.caption:
Is water wet? 💧

In science, wetting is what a liquid does to a surface. By that rule, water makes other things wet.

Dictionaries split. Dictionary.com says wet means moistened, covered or soaked. Wiktionary says it can mean made up of liquid, and by that rule water is wet.

Our verdict: wet is what happens to the dry thing. Team Wet or Team Not Wet? 👇

Sources: USGS; Wikipedia (Wetting); Dictionary.com; Wiktionary.
reels.alt_text: Cut-paper animation. A frowning water drop asks if it is wet. Drops soak a towel, a drop spreads on one surface and beads on another, a dictionary opens, and a verdict reads: wet is what happens to the dry thing.

reels.title: Same Question, Different World 3: Sunsets
reels.hook: On Mars, the sunset is blue.
reels.caption:
On Mars, the sunset is blue. 🔵

Earth's air scatters blue away, so red gets through. Martian dust is fine enough to let blue through best and keep it near the Sun. Curiosity saw it in color on April 15, 2015.

Uranus here is a NASA simulation. The Moon's sky just stays black.

Same Question, Different World, part 3. Next: snow. Which sunset would you watch? 👇

Sources: NASA; JPL; Royal Museums Greenwich.

reels.title: Same Question, Different World 4: Snow
reels.hook: On Mars, snowflakes may be cubes.
reels.caption:
On Mars, snowflakes may be cubes. 🧊

Earth's have six sides because of how water molecules line up. Mars also has dry-ice snow, and its fourfold symmetry means scientists expect tiny cubes. As of 2022, nobody had pictured it falling.

On Enceladus, jets spray ice and most falls back like snow.

Same Question, Different World, part 4. Next: how long is a day? 👇

Sources: NASA JPL; NASA; NOAA.
